subtopic_detail: a young man seeking rhinoplasty for a defect others cannot see, with three hours daily of mirror checking
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 22 year old apprentice electrician who asks for a referral to a plastic surgeon. He believes the bridge of his nose is twisted and that people stare at it.

He spends about three hours a day checking his profile in mirrors and in the reflective glass of shop windows, takes photographs from different angles to compare, and has stopped going to his football club social nights. He has cancelled two family gatherings in the past month. He has no concerns about his weight, eats normally and his body mass index is 23 kg/m2. He accepts that his family and friends tell him his nose looks ordinary but says he cannot make himself believe it. On examination his nose is symmetrical with no deviation.

data_table.Examination: Nasal bridge straight and symmetrical, no septal deviation, no excoriation of the skin

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Refer to a plastic surgeon for an opinion on corrective rhinoplasty
options.rationale: Cosmetic surgery in this setting rarely satisfies the patient and the preoccupation typically transfers to the operated site or to a new body part, with worsening distress afterwards. Surgery would only be appropriate if there were an objective deformity, which examination has excluded. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Commence olanzapine at low dose for a fixed belief about his body
options.rationale: Poor insight is common in this disorder and does not by itself make the belief delusional or make an antipsychotic the right treatment, since these patients respond to the same therapy as those with better insight. An antipsychotic is considered only as augmentation when a serotonergic drug and therapy have failed. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy adapted to appearance concerns
options.rationale: Cognitive behavioural therapy incorporating exposure to avoided situations and prevention of mirror checking and reassurance seeking is the recommended first treatment and targets the maintaining behaviours directly. Perceptual retraining in front of a mirror is a specific component that ordinary anxiety focused therapy does not include. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Reassure him about his appearance and review again in three months
options.rationale: Reassurance is itself one of the behaviours that maintains the disorder, giving brief relief followed by renewed doubt and more checking, so repeating it in the consulting room strengthens the cycle. He has already told you that family reassurance does not hold. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

options.text: Start fluoxetine and arrange psychological review only if it fails
options.rationale: A serotonin reuptake inhibitor at the higher doses used for obsessive compulsive spectrum disorders is an effective treatment and is combined with therapy in moderate to severe illness, but it is not preferred over therapy as the sole opening move. This would be the right answer if therapy were unavailable or he declined it. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

explanation.summary: Body dysmorphic disorder is a preoccupation with a perceived defect that is unobservable or slight to others, combined with repetitive behaviours such as mirror checking, comparing, camouflaging or reassurance seeking. It typically begins in adolescence and is under recognised because patients present to dermatologists and surgeons rather than to mental health services. The nose, skin and hair are the most commonly targeted areas, and muscle dysmorphia is a recognised variant in young men. Suicidal ideation and attempts are substantially more frequent than in obsessive compulsive disorder, so risk assessment is part of every review. Insight is often poor and up to a third of patients hold the belief with delusional intensity, which changes neither the diagnosis nor the first line treatment.
key_points: The defect is absent or slight to an observer while the distress is severe
Repetitive checking, comparing or camouflaging is required for the diagnosis
Cosmetic procedures usually leave the preoccupation unchanged or worse
Cognitive behavioural therapy with response prevention is first line
Suicide risk is high and is assessed at every contact
explanation.pearls: Serotonin reuptake inhibitors for body dysmorphic disorder need obsessive compulsive range doses, for example fluoxetine 40 to 80 mg daily, and a twelve week trial before the response is judged, which is longer and higher than the usual depression trial.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

subtopic_detail: sleepiness on night duty with an inability to sleep during the day in a rotating roster worker whose sleep is normal on leave
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 34 year old intensive care nurse who has worked a rotating roster with blocks of four night shifts for the past eight months. She asks for something to help her sleep.

She describes lying awake until midday after a night shift, managing only three to four broken hours, and then fighting to stay awake from about three in the morning on the next shift. She has twice caught herself drifting at the wheel on the drive home. On her two week annual leave in April she slept seven to eight hours a night without difficulty and felt well. She does not snore, has no witnessed pauses in breathing, and her body mass index is 22 kg/m2. Her partner sleeps in the same room and reports no kicking or restless movements.

data_table.Examination: Mallampati class 1, neck circumference 32 cm, no goitre, mood and cognition normal
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, iron studies including ferritin and thyroid stimulating hormone all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Prescribe zopiclone to be taken before each daytime sleep period
options.rationale: A hypnotic may lengthen the daytime sleep a little but does nothing for the sleepiness on shift, which is the part that is putting her at risk on the road, and tolerance and dependence follow regular use. Sedatives are a short term adjunct at most, not the opening move. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Refer for overnight polysomnography before any treatment is started
options.rationale: A sleep study is indicated when obstructive sleep apnoea, narcolepsy or a periodic limb movement disorder is suspected, and a body mass index of 22 with no snoring, no witnessed apnoea and no limb movements makes those unlikely. The normal sleep on annual leave points firmly to a circadian rather than an intrinsic sleep disorder. (Source: Sleep Health Foundation Australia)

options.text: Prescribe modafinil each night shift and arrange follow up in a month
options.rationale: A wake promoting agent reduces sleepiness during night work but is reserved for residual impairment after circadian and behavioural measures have been optimised, and in Australia its subsidised indications do not cover this disorder. It would be considered if the structured programme below failed. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Plan timed bright light, protected daytime sleep and a pre shift nap
options.rationale: Shifting the circadian clock with bright light early in the shift, dark glasses for the drive home, a blacked out and quiet sleep period with the phone off, and a planned nap before the shift is the first line package and addresses both the insomnia and the sleepiness. It also directly reduces the drive home risk she has already had two warnings about. (Source: Sleep Health Foundation Australia)

options.text: Commence melatonin at bedtime and review her sleep diary in six weeks
options.rationale: Melatonin taken before the daytime sleep can help consolidate it and is a reasonable adjunct, but used alone and at the wrong clock time it shifts the rhythm unpredictably and leaves the on shift sleepiness untreated. Its timing relative to the desired sleep period matters more than the dose. (Source: Sleep Health Foundation Australia)

explanation.summary: Shift work disorder is diagnosed when insomnia or excessive sleepiness is temporally linked to a work schedule that overlaps the usual sleep period, persists for at least three months, and is not better explained by another sleep disorder. The discriminating history is that sleep normalises on leave or on a run of day shifts, which separates a circadian misalignment from a primary insomnia. Around a fifth to a quarter of shift workers meet criteria, and night shift, early morning starts and rapidly rotating rosters carry the highest risk. Drowsy driving on the commute home is the most immediate danger and should be asked about explicitly, along with an offer of alternative transport arrangements. Longer term associations include cardiometabolic disease and mood disorder, which is why roster design is part of management rather than an aside.
key_points: Sleep that normalises on annual leave points to a circadian rather than intrinsic disorder
Ask directly about drowsy driving on the commute home
Bright light early in the shift and dark glasses afterwards shift the clock in the wanted direction
Protect the daytime sleep period with darkness, quiet and a silenced phone
Hypnotics and wake promoting drugs follow rather than replace circadian measures
explanation.pearls: A planned nap of 20 to 30 minutes taken before the night shift, or in the first half of it, improves alertness without the deep sleep inertia that follows a nap longer than about 45 minutes.

subtopic_detail: persistent detachment and a flat unreal quality to the world after a single cannabis episode, with reality testing preserved
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar assessing a 20 year old university student referred by his general practitioner. Eight months ago, at a party, he smoked a much stronger cannabis preparation than he was used to and felt intensely frightened for several hours.

Since that night he has felt, in his words, like he is watching himself from just behind his own shoulder, and says his hands sometimes look as though they belong to someone else. Colours seem washed out and the street where he grew up looks like a stage set. He finds all of this distressing and says he knows perfectly well that it is his own mind playing tricks and that the world has not really changed. He has not used cannabis or any other substance since that night. He has no gaps in his memory for events or for personal information, hears no voices and holds no unusual beliefs.

data_table.Examination: Cooperative, reactive affect, speech normal in rate and form, no thought disorder, cognition intact
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen negative, full blood count, urea electrolytes and creatinine and thyroid stimulating hormone all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Cannabis induced psychotic disorder with residual perceptual features
options.rationale: A substance induced psychotic disorder requires hallucinations or delusions, and it is the preserved reality testing that excludes it: he describes the experience as if rather than asserting that the world has changed. A drug episode is nonetheless the single most common trigger for the correct condition. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

options.text: Persistent depersonalisation and derealisation disorder after cannabis
options.rationale: Persistent or recurrent detachment from one's own body or mental processes together with unreality of surroundings, with intact reality testing and clinically significant distress, defines this disorder, and cannabis is the commonest precipitant in young men. The absence of memory gaps, voices and unusual beliefs rules out the competing diagnoses. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

options.text: Panic disorder presenting with prominent dissociative experiences
options.rationale: Depersonalisation is a recognised symptom during a panic attack, but it is then episodic and tied to discrete surges of autonomic arousal rather than continuously present for eight months. He describes no palpitations, breathlessness or crescendo fear episodes. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Schizophrenia presenting with predominantly negative and odd symptoms
options.rationale: Negative symptoms involve genuine loss of volition, affect and speech output, whereas he is distressed by and fully aware of a change in the quality of his experience, which is a different phenomenon. His reactive affect and intact thought form argue against it. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

options.text: Post traumatic stress disorder of the dissociative subtype after a scare
options.rationale: The dissociative subtype sits on top of a full post traumatic syndrome, which requires re experiencing, avoidance of trauma reminders, negative cognitions and hyperarousal, none of which he reports. The frightening drug episode is a trigger for the dissociative state rather than an index trauma driving intrusions. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Depersonalisation and derealisation disorder is common enough to affect roughly one to two per cent of the population yet is routinely misdiagnosed as psychosis, because clinicians hear the strangeness of the description rather than the preserved insight within it. The distinguishing feature is the as if quality: the patient knows the experience is generated by their own mind, which is exactly what a psychotic patient does not. Onset clusters in late adolescence and early adulthood, and cannabis, hallucinogens, severe anxiety and sleep deprivation are the usual precipitants. Explaining the phenomenon and its benign nature is itself therapeutic because much of the distress comes from fear of going mad. No drug is specifically approved, and treatment targets comorbid anxiety and depression alongside psychological therapy.
key_points: Intact reality testing is what separates this disorder from psychosis
Cannabis is the single commonest precipitant in young people
Absence of memory gaps excludes dissociative amnesia and identity disorder
Psychoeducation reduces the secondary fear that drives much of the distress
Treat comorbid anxiety and depression, which are present in most cases
explanation.pearls: Antipsychotics do not help this disorder and frequently worsen the subjective deadness, so a diagnostic trial of one is not a harmless way of resolving uncertainty about whether the presentation is psychotic.

subtopic_detail: a severely neglected preschooler in foster care whose social reciprocity is improving with placement rather than remaining fixed
stem:
You are the registrar in a child development clinic seeing a 4 year old boy placed with a foster carer eighteen months ago. Before the placement he lived in conditions of severe neglect with several changes of caregiver.

The referral says he seldom goes to an adult for comfort when he falls and rarely responds when his carer tries to soothe him, and that he shows little positive emotion during play. His carer adds that in the past six months he has begun to bring her drawings unprompted, glances back at her when something surprises him, and has started feeding a toy dinosaur with a plastic spoon. His vocabulary and sentence structure are appropriate for his age and he understands two step instructions. He lines his cars up occasionally but plays with them as cars as well, and he has no repetitive mannerisms and no sensory aversions.

data_table.Examination: Subdued affect, limited comfort seeking, emerging shared attention with the carer, growth on the fiftieth centile
data_table.Investigations: Hearing and vision screening both within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Autism spectrum disorder with an associated language strength profile
options.rationale: Autism requires persistent deficits in social communication together with restricted or repetitive behaviours, and the emerging joint attention, spontaneous showing and symbolic pretend play since placement point away from it. The steady improvement in reciprocity as caregiving improved is the discriminator, since autistic social differences do not resolve with a change of carer. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Global developmental delay arising from prolonged early understimulation
options.rationale: Global delay requires significant impairment across two or more developmental domains, and his language, comprehension and growth are all age appropriate. Neglect can certainly cause delay, but here the deficit is confined to the attachment and emotional domain. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Disinhibited social engagement disorder following the early deprivation
options.rationale: The disinhibited form presents as overfamiliarity, with a child who wanders off with strangers and shows no reticence, which is the mirror image of the withdrawn picture described here. Both follow deprivation, but they are distinguished by whether the child approaches too readily or not at all. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

options.text: Childhood depressive disorder with marked anhedonia and social withdrawal
options.rationale: Depression in a preschooler would show a change from a previous better state with disturbance of sleep, appetite and play, whereas his reduced positive affect has been present since infancy and is improving rather than worsening. The developmental history of pathogenic care is what reframes it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Reactive attachment disorder arising from grossly insufficient early care
options.rationale: A consistently inhibited and emotionally withdrawn pattern toward caregivers, minimal comfort seeking and response to comfort, and reduced positive affect in a child with a documented history of grossly inadequate care defines this disorder. The improvement with an adequate carer is characteristic and is exactly what distinguishes it from autism. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

explanation.summary: Reactive attachment disorder can only be diagnosed where there is a documented history of pathogenic care, meaning persistent social neglect, repeated changes of primary caregiver, or rearing in a setting that prevented selective attachments forming. The child must have a developmental age of at least nine months so that selective attachment would normally have been established, and the picture must not be better explained by autism. Distinguishing the two is the central clinical task and is often got wrong in both directions, with consequences for the services a child is offered. The practical test is responsiveness to improved caregiving: attachment difficulties soften over months in a stable placement whereas autistic social communication differences persist. Treatment is not individual therapy for the child but work with the caregiver to build sensitive, predictable, responsive care, and placement stability is the single most powerful intervention available.
key_points: A history of grossly insufficient care is a required criterion, not merely supportive
The withdrawn form is reactive attachment disorder, the overfamiliar form is disinhibited social engagement disorder
Improvement with a stable sensitive carer argues strongly against autism
Symbolic pretend play and spontaneous showing are evidence against autism
Treatment works through the caregiver relationship, not through therapy delivered to the child alone
explanation.pearls: Disinhibited social engagement disorder persists in a proportion of children even after attachment security is achieved with a new carer, whereas reactive attachment disorder characteristically remits once care improves, so the two differ in prognosis as well as presentation.

Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline

subtopic_detail: yearning and preoccupation sixteen months after a spousal death that has not moved despite an adequate antidepressant trial
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 58 year old woman whose husband died sixteen months ago after a short illness. She was started on sertraline by a colleague six months ago and has taken 100 mg daily for the past four months without missing doses.

She describes an ache of longing for him that fills most of the day, spends hours going through his photographs and messages, and has not been able to open the door of his study. She says she still cannot take in that he is gone. She lights up describing her granddaughter's swimming carnival last weekend and went to it willingly. She eats normally, her weight is unchanged, she feels she was a good wife and she has no thoughts of harming herself. There is no psychomotor slowing and she is not self critical.

data_table.Examination: Tearful when speaking of her husband, warm and reactive otherwise, no psychomotor retardation, cognition intact
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, urea electrolytes and creatinine, thyroid stimulating hormone and vitamin B12 all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Refer for a structured psychological therapy targeting her grief
options.rationale: Grief focused psychotherapy, which combines revisiting the death with graded approach to avoided reminders and work on restoring goals, outperforms antidepressants for this condition and is the recommended treatment. The avoided study door is precisely the kind of target the approach component addresses. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

options.text: Increase the sertraline to 150 mg daily and review her again in six weeks
options.rationale: Dose escalation is the right move in a depressive episode with a partial response, but her presentation lacks pervasive anhedonia, worthlessness and appetite change, and antidepressants have not been shown to reduce the core yearning and preoccupation of this condition. Four months at a therapeutic dose without movement is itself evidence the target is wrong. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Add low dose quetiapine at night to settle her ruminative preoccupation
options.rationale: Augmenting with an antipsychotic is a strategy for treatment resistant depression with an established diagnosis, not for grief, and it adds metabolic and sedative burden without addressing avoidance. Preoccupation with a deceased person is not the rumination of a depressive illness. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Reassure her that this is normal bereavement and review in six months
options.rationale: Intense yearning with preoccupation, disbelief and avoidance persisting beyond twelve months after the death in an adult, at a level that impairs function, is past the boundary of expected grief and is a recognised disorder in its own right. Normalising it here delays effective treatment for a woman who has already waited sixteen months. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

options.text: Refer her to a community bereavement support group as the only measure
options.rationale: Peer support groups help many bereaved people and are valuable alongside treatment, but trials show they do not resolve the established disorder and can reinforce avoidance if the group does not work with it. Generic support is not equivalent to a structured therapy with a defined protocol. (Source: Australian Centre for Grief and Bereavement)
source_refs: Australian Centre for Grief and Bereavement

explanation.summary: Prolonged grief disorder is defined by persistent intense yearning or preoccupation with the deceased, accompanied by features such as disbelief, identity disruption, emotional numbness, avoidance of reminders and difficulty re engaging with life, causing impairment and lasting beyond twelve months after the death in an adult. The twelve month threshold is deliberately conservative because most bereaved people improve without treatment, and only a minority of around one in ten develop the persistent form. The frequent clinical error is to treat it as a depressive episode, since the phenomenology differs: sadness is focused on the lost person rather than pervasive, self esteem is usually intact, and positive emotion remains accessible in other domains. That distinction matters because antidepressants do not treat the core symptoms whereas targeted psychotherapy does. Risk factors include a sudden or violent death, loss of a child or partner, and a pre existing anxiety or mood disorder.
key_points: The adult threshold is twelve months from the death, not six
Grief is focused on the deceased, whereas depressive anhedonia is pervasive
Preserved self esteem and preserved capacity for pleasure argue against a depressive episode
Avoidance of reminders maintains the disorder and is the main therapeutic target
Antidepressants do not reduce yearning and preoccupation on current evidence
explanation.pearls: Prolonged grief disorder requires the death to have occurred at least twelve months earlier in adults but only six months earlier in children and adolescents, which is a commonly missed distinction when assessing a bereaved young person.

Australian Centre for Grief and Bereavement
